title: Drawing Your Thinking
tagline: A naturalist's notebook and a branching drawing: how to see the shape of a subject on one page, and then walk through it.
card: Why a branching map beats a page of notes, and how to turn any map into a memory palace.
goal: you will learn the rules of a good mind map, draw the branches of a subject on one page, and turn the map into a palace with a room for each branch.

left_off.q: What are the five canons of rhetoric?
left_off.a: Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery.

left_off.q: What do you memorise for a talk, in the palace method?
left_off.a: A picture for each main point, placed along a route; not the script.
A picture that tells you where to restart if your mind goes blank.

text: London, July 1837. A young naturalist, Charles Darwin, has been back from his long voyage on the Beagle for less than a year. His head is full of facts: finches from one island and mockingbirds from another, fossils, shells, bones, and a question he is not sure he dares to ask. His notebooks are full of lists.
On one page of a small notebook he stops listing. He writes two words at the top, I think, and underneath he draws something that is not a list at all.

check.q: What did Darwin do differently on that page?
check.a: He stopped writing a list and drew a branching shape.

parts.talk: When you think hard about something, do you write lists, draw pictures, or talk? Which helps you most?

text: It is a small, rough drawing: a single line that splits, and splits again, like the branches of a tree. Some of the branches end. Some keep going. It shows his idea that all living things are related, descending from common ancestors, with new kinds branching off over time.

The drawing is famous today. It shows the thing a list cannot show: how ideas connect. A list puts every item in a row, and every item looks the same size. A branching drawing shows which things belong together, which come first, and which are the trunk and which only twigs.

check.q: What does a branching drawing show that a list cannot?
check.a: How things connect: which belong together, which come first, and which are main branches and which twigs.

parts.talk: Think of a subject you know well. How would it look as a tree, with the trunk, the big branches and the twigs?

text: In the 1970s the writer and educator Tony Buzan popularised a way of taking notes in this branching form, which he called mind mapping. He explained it in a BBC series, Use Your Head, and in a book of the same name. A mind map starts from one central idea and spreads out in all directions, with a key word on every line.
A map is a good memory tool for another reason. It is a picture of a subject, and you already know what to do with pictures. In this lesson you will draw one and then turn it into a house.

check.q: Who popularised mind mapping, and where did he explain it?
check.a: Tony Buzan, in the 1970s, in a BBC series and a book called Use Your Head.

parts.talk: Have you ever used a mind map for study or work? What was it like?

words.m: a part that grows out of a main stem. The map has five main branches.
a system in which things are arranged by importance, from top to bottom.
one important word that carries the meaning of a longer idea.
spreading out from a centre like the spokes of a wheel.
to come from an earlier source. Species descend from common ancestors.

source: Darwin's 1837 'I think' tree is in his Notebook B. Tony Buzan's Use Your Head series was broadcast by the BBC in 1974. Retold here in our own words.
method_heading: The rules of a good map

method.x: A mind map is a single page with a central image in the middle and branches spreading out from it. Each branch carries one idea; smaller branches carry details.

data.label: A mind map of the five main branches of philosophy

method.cap: A subject on one page: centre, five main branches, and one detail on each.

items.x: Draw the main idea as a picture or a word in a shape. Use the whole page.

items.h: Give each main idea its own branch.
items.x: Three to seven main branches is a good number.

items.h: Use one key word per line.
items.x: Not sentences. Keep the words short and write them on the branch.
Each sub-branch comes from a main branch.
A different colour for each main branch.

method.x: A map shows you the structure. A palace lets you keep it. The two fit together because both are made of places.

items.h: Choose a palace with a room for each main branch.
Turn each branch into a picture and put it in its room.
items.x: Metaphysics could be a huge glowing question mark floating over the hall.

items.h: Turn each sub-branch into a picture in a place within the room.
items.x: Detail goes on furniture and walls.
From room to room, branch by branch.

method.title: Philosophy in five rooms
lines: A glowing question mark floats in the hall, and the floor keeps turning transparent so you see what is real underneath.
A giant eye on a desk is reading a book and peeping through a magnifying glass.
A tray of food is being shared out fairly, with a pair of scales on the table.
A neat chain of train carriages runs under the bed, each linked to the next with a ticket.
A beautiful painting of a sunset is hanging from a tree.
method.pic: One page, five rooms: you can look at a subject, and then walk through it.

method.x:
map it to see it.
palace it to keep it.
Say aloud the five branches of philosophy, one question for each, and the room you would put each in.

try.title: Branches and questions
try.prompt: Match each branch of philosophy to its main question.

try.title: Make your own map
try.prompt: Choose a subject you know well (a hobby, a job, a place). On paper, draw a central image and at least four main branches, each with one key word and two details. Then write the branches here.
try.model: Centre: Cooking. Branches: Equipment (knives, pans), Methods (roast, boil, fry), Ingredients (veg, meat, spices), Meals (breakfast, lunch, dinner). Colour-code each branch.
checks: I have at least four main branches.
Each branch has a short key word, not a sentence.

try.title: Turn it into a palace
try.prompt: Take your map. Choose a palace with the same number of rooms, and write a picture for each branch, placed in its room.
try.model: Hall: Equipment, a knife the size of a car on the doormat. Kitchen: Methods, a pan dancing on the stove. Pantry: Ingredients, a pile of vegetables with sunglasses. Dining room: Meals, a table laid for the whole street.
checks: The rooms are in order along my route.

items.s: A mind map starts with a ___ image in the middle of the page.
To turn a map into a palace, give each main branch its own ___.

try.q: Why is a mind map better than a list for seeing a subject?
opts: It shows how things connect, and which are main branches
try.why: A list puts every item in a row; a map shows the shape of the subject.

try.title: Explain your map
try.prompt: Describe your map aloud: the centre, each branch, and why you put the branches where you did.

cards: A one-page map of a subject: central image, branches, key words.
One big idea coming straight from the centre. Three to seven.
One short word that carries a bigger idea.
A room for each main branch, a place for each sub-branch.
A 1837 sketch of branching descent, headed 'I think'.
Popularised mind mapping in the 1970s; BBC series Use Your Head.

quiz.q: How many main branches does a map usually have?
quiz.why: Enough to organise, few enough to see at a glance.
Short key words keep the map clear.

quiz.q: In a palace conversion, what does a main branch become?
quiz.why: Each main branch becomes a room.

quiz.q: What does a branching drawing show that a list does not?

challenge.title: Memory challenge: the five branches
challenge.intro: Learn the five branches of philosophy in order, one in each of five rooms. Metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, logic, aesthetics.
challenge.study: Use the five rooms from the example, or your own. A picture for each, and one question for each.

What is the King of Clubs in the card system?

A place on the palace route where a picture sits.
